common_name: Shirofugen Flowering Cherry (Late-Blooming Double Pink-and-White Cherry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Shirofugen is among the last of the ornamental cherries to bloom each season, extending the flowering-cherry display well after Yoshino and Kwanzan have finished.

directions: Shirofugen opens rich pink from coppery-bronze new foliage, then fades through the bloom period to nearly white before finishing with a faint pink flush, giving a single tree two or three distinct color phases over its unusually long, late-spring flowering window. The large double flowers hang in long-stalked clusters and the tree matures into a broad, flat-topped, wide-spreading canopy that is often nearly as wide as it is tall, so give it generous room away from structures and walkways. Provide moist, well-drained soil in full sun and avoid heavy pruning except right after bloom, since large wounds invite the canker and borer problems that shorten the lifespan of most ornamental cherries.

common_name: Shirotae Flowering Cherry (Mount Fuji Cherry, Fragrant White Weeping-Branched Cherry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Shirotae (sold in the US as 'Mount Fuji') develops a wide, flat-topped, horizontally tiered branch structure, so choose an open site rather than a tight corner.

directions: Shirotae carries large, semi-double to double pure-white flowers with a light almond-like fragrance, opening in drooping clusters along branches that spread horizontally in flat, layered tiers rather than growing strongly upward, so the tree typically ends up wider than it is tall. Fresh green young foliage rather than the bronze new growth seen in many other cherry cultivars keeps the emerging leaves from competing visually with the white bloom. Site it in full sun with moist, well-drained soil and enough lateral space for the spreading tiers to develop without crowding, and prune only immediately after flowering to reduce disease entry.

common_name: Amanogawa Flowering Cherry (Columnar Upright Fragrant Cherry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Amanogawa's narrow, columnar growth habit makes it one of the few ornamental cherries suited to tight side yards, driveway strips, and other narrow planting spaces.

directions: Amanogawa is the classic fastigiate flowering cherry, its branches held tightly upright to form a narrow column rather than the broad, spreading canopy typical of most ornamental cherries, making it useful for framing entries or lining narrow spaces where a normal cherry would outgrow the site. The semi-double, pale pink flowers carry a light fragrance and cluster densely along the vertical branches in mid-spring. Because the upright form is achieved through unusually tight branch angles, occasional thinning after bloom helps prevent included bark and narrow crotch failures as the tree ages; plant in full sun with moist, well-drained soil for best form and flowering density.

common_name: Shogetsu Flowering Cherry (Shimidsu Sakura, Frilly Double White Cherry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Shogetsu (also sold as 'Shimidsu Sakura') is one of the latest cherries to flower, so it pairs well with earlier cultivars like Yoshino to extend the bloom season.

directions: Shogetsu opens from deep pink buds into large, fully double flowers that fade to nearly white, and the unusually long flower stalks give the pendant clusters a loose, frilly appearance distinct from the tighter pompom look of Kwanzan. Growth is low and umbrella-shaped, spreading wider than tall, which makes it a good choice for a specimen tree in a lawn or border where its full canopy can be viewed from below. Give it full sun and moist, well-drained soil, and prune conservatively right after flowering since the wide, low branching is part of the tree's characteristic silhouette.

common_name: Ukon Flowering Cherry (Rare Greenish-Yellow Ornamental Cherry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Ukon is grown specifically for its unusual pale greenish-yellow flower color, a rarity among ornamental cherries that are otherwise almost entirely pink or white.

directions: Ukon stands apart from other flowering cherries with semi-double blooms in an unusual pale creamy yellow-green rather than the pink or white shades typical of the group, an effect most pronounced as the flowers first open and fading toward white as they age. Coppery-bronze young foliage emerges alongside the flowers and later turns purplish in autumn, adding a second season of color. Plant in full sun with moist, well-drained soil and give it the same broad, upright-spreading canopy space as other Japanese flowering cherries, since its habit closely resembles Kwanzan aside from the distinctive bloom color.

common_name: Royal Burgundy Flowering Cherry (Purple-Leaved Double Pink Cherry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Royal Burgundy is a purple-leaved sport of Kwanzan and needs strong sun exposure to hold its deep burgundy foliage color rather than fading toward green.

directions: Royal Burgundy combines double, rosy-pink spring flowers with foliage that emerges deep reddish-purple and holds that color through most of the growing season, giving it a longer window of ornamental interest than green-leaved cherries whose color impact is limited to the bloom period. The upright, vase-shaped habit and lack of significant fruit set mirror its parent cultivar Kwanzan, from which it arose as a foliage-color sport. Grow it in full sun on moist, well-drained soil, since shaded plantings cause the purple leaf color to wash out toward green, and prune only right after flowering to limit canker and borer entry points typical of ornamental cherries.

common_name: Akebono Yoshino Cherry (Daybreak Cherry, Pink-Flowered Yoshino Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Akebono (also sold as 'Daybreak') is a pink-flowered Yoshino selection that tolerates the mild winters of warmer zones better than the straight species, making it a common choice for West Coast and southern plantings.

directions: Akebono blooms with the same profuse, early-spring flush as standard Yoshino cherry but in a soft pink that fades to blush white as flowers age, giving slightly more color impact from a distance than the nearly white species form. Its rounded, wide-spreading canopy and slightly more compact stature than seedling-grown Yoshino make it a popular street and park tree selection. Plant in full sun with moist, well-drained soil, and expect the same relatively short 15-20 year typical lifespan and susceptibility to canker and borers common to ornamental flowering cherries.

common_name: Weeping Higan Cherry (Pendula, Classic Cascading Spring-Flowering Cherry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped grafted trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; 'Pendula' is typically top-grafted onto a standard trunk, so the graft union should be checked periodically and any upright, non-weeping shoots below it removed.

directions: Pendula produces slender, cascading branches that reach the ground in mature specimens, covered in single to semi-double pale pink flowers that emerge before the leaves in early spring for an especially graceful, fountain-like display. The weeping habit is most dramatic when the tree is grafted high on a standard trunk, so choose a specimen with a tall, clear graft point if a strongly cascading form is the goal. Site it in full sun on moist, well-drained soil with open space on all sides so the sweeping branches can develop unobstructed, and remove any vigorous upright suckers that emerge from the rootstock below the graft.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Autumnalis is prized for producing a partial flush of flowers in mild fall and winter weather in addition to its main spring bloom, unlike most flowering cherries that bloom only once.

directions: Autumnalis carries semi-double, pale pink flowers that appear intermittently through fall and mild winter stretches whenever temperatures rise enough to trigger a flush, then finishes with a fuller display in early spring, giving it a much longer effective bloom season than a single-flush cherry. The rounded, twiggy, upright-spreading canopy is more refined and less dense than the double-flowered cultivars, and the tree is somewhat more cold-hardy and longer-lived than many showy ornamental cherries. Grow it in full sun on moist, well-drained soil, and expect the fall flowering to be sparser and more sporadic than the concentrated spring flush, varying from year to year with autumn weather patterns.
